{{Short description|Cubic polynomials defined from a monic polynomial of degree four}}
[[File:Resolvente.png|thumb|right|upright=1.5|Graph of the polynomial function {{math|''x''<sup>4</sup> + ''x''<sup>3</sup> – ''x''<sup>2</sup> – 7''x''/4 – 1/2}} (in green) together with the graph of its resolvent cubic {{math|''R''<sub>4</sub>(''y'')}} (in red). The roots of both polynomials are visible too.]]
In [[algebra]], a '''resolvent cubic''' is one of several distinct, although related, [[cubic function|cubic polynomials]] defined from a [[monic polynomial|monic]] [[quartic function|polynomial of degree four]]:

:<math>P(x)=x^4+a_3x^3+a_2x^2+a_1x+a_0.</math>

In each case:
* The coefficients of the resolvent cubic can be obtained from the coefficients of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} using only sums, subtractions and multiplications.
* Knowing the roots of the resolvent cubic of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is useful for finding the roots of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} itself. Hence the name “resolvent cubic”.
* The polynomial {{math|''P''(''x'')}} has a [[Multiplicity (mathematics)#Multiplicity of a root of a polynomial|multiple root]] [[if and only if]] its resolvent cubic has a multiple root.

==Definitions==
Suppose that the coefficients of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} belong to a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] {{math|''k''}} whose [[Characteristic (algebra)#Case of fields|characteristic]] is different from&nbsp;{{math|2}}. Whenever roots of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} are mentioned, they belong to some [[Field extension|extension]] {{math|''K''}} of {{math|''k''}} such that {{math|''P''(''x'')}} factors into linear factors in {{math|''K''[''x'']}}. If {{math|''k''}} is the field {{math|'''Q'''}} of rational numbers, then {{mvar|K}} can be the field {{math|'''C'''}} of [[Complex number|complex numbers]] or the field {{overline|{{math|'''Q'''}}}} of [[algebraic number]]s.

In some cases, the concept of resolvent cubic is defined only when {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is a quartic in depressed form—that is, when {{math|''a''<sub>3</sub>&nbsp;{{=}}&nbsp;0}}.

Note that the [[Resolvent cubic#Fourth definition|fourth]] and [[Resolvent cubic#Fifth definition|fifth]] definitions below also make sense and that the relationship between these resolvent cubics and {{math|''P''(''x'')}} are still valid if the characteristic of {{mvar|k}} is equal to&nbsp;{{math|2}}.

===First definition===
Suppose that {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is a depressed quartic—that is, that {{math|''a''<sub>3</sub> {{=}} 0}}. A possible definition of the resolvent cubic of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is:<ref name="Tignol">{{Citation|last = Tignol|first = Jean-Pierre| author-link=Jean-Pierre Tignol |title=Galois' Theory of algebraic equations|edition = 2nd|publisher = [[World Scientific]]|year = 2016|chapter = Quartic equations|isbn = 978-981-4704-69-4|zbl = 1333.12001}}</ref>

:<math>R_1(y)=8y^3+8a_2y^2+(2{a_2}^2-8a_0)y-{a_1}^2.</math>

The origin of this definition lies in applying [[Quartic function#Ferrari's solution|Ferrari's method]] to find the roots of {{math|''P''(''x'')}}. To be more precise:

:<math>\begin{align}P(x)=0&\Longleftrightarrow x^4+a_2x^2=-a_1x-a_0\\ &\Longleftrightarrow
\left(x^2+\frac{a_2}2\right)^2=-a_1x-a_0+\frac{{a_2}^2}4.\end{align}</math>

Add a new unknown, {{mvar|y}}, to {{math|''x''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''a''<sub>2</sub>/2}}. Now you have:

:<math>\begin{align}\left(x^2+\frac{a_2}2+y\right)^2&=-a_1x-a_0+\frac{{a_2}^2}4+2x^2y+a_2y+y^2\\
&=2yx^2-a_1x-a_0+\frac{{a_2}^2}4+a_2y+y^2.\end{align}</math>

If this expression is a square, it can only be the square of

:<math>\sqrt{2y}\,x-\frac{a_1}{2\sqrt{2y}}.</math>

But the equality

:<math>\left(\sqrt{2y}\,x-\frac{a_1}{2\sqrt{2y}}\right)^2=2yx^2-a_1x-a_0+\frac{{a_2}^2}4+a_2y+y^2</math>

is equivalent to

:<math>\frac{{a_1}^2}{8y}=-a_0+\frac{{a_2}^2}4+a_2y+y^2\text{,}</math>

and this is the same thing as the assertion that {{math|''R''<sub>1</sub>(''y'')}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.

If {{math|''y''<sub>0</sub>}} is a root of {{math|''R''<sub>1</sub>(''y'')}}, then it is a consequence of the computations made above that the roots of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} are the roots of the polynomial

:<math>x^2-\sqrt{2y_0}\,x+\frac{a_2}2+y_0+\frac{a_1}{2\sqrt{2y_0}}</math>

together with the roots of the polynomial

:<math>x^2+\sqrt{2y_0}\,x+\frac{a_2}2+y_0-\frac{a_1}{2\sqrt{2y_0}}.</math>

Of course, this makes no sense if {{math|''y''<sub>0</sub> {{=}} 0}}, but since the [[constant term]] of {{math|''R''<sub>1</sub>(''y'')}} is {{math|–''a''<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>}}, {{math|0}} is a root of {{math|''R''<sub>1</sub>(''y'')}} if and only if {{math|''a''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} 0}}, and in this case the roots of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} can be found using the [[quadratic formula]].

===Second definition===
Another possible definition<ref name="Tignol"/> (still supposing that {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is a depressed quartic) is

:<math>R_2(y)=8y^3-4a_2y^2-8a_0y+4a_2a_0-{a_1}^2</math>

The origin of this definition is similar to the previous one. This time, we start by doing:

:<math>\begin{align}P(x)=0&\Longleftrightarrow x^4=-a_2x^2-a_1x-a_0\\ &\Longleftrightarrow(x^2+y)^2=-a_2x^2-a_1x-a_0+2yx^2+y^2\end{align}</math>

and a computation similar to the previous one shows that this last expression is a square if and only if

:<math>8y^3-4a_2y^2-8a_0y+4a_2a_0-{a_1}^2=0\text{.}</math>

A simple computation shows that

:<math>R_2\left(y+\frac{a_2}2\right)=R_1(y).</math>

===Third definition===
Another possible definition<ref name="Brookfield">{{Citation | author=Brookfield, G. | title=Factoring quartic polynomials: A lost art | journal=[[Mathematics Magazine]] | volume=80 | issue=1 | year=2007 | pages=67–70 | doi=10.1080/0025570X.2007.11953453 | jstor=27642994 | url=http://web.calstatela.edu/faculty/gbrookf/pubs/quartic.pdf | zbl=1227.97040 | s2cid=53375377 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150221005838/http://web.calstatela.edu/faculty/gbrookf/pubs/quartic.pdf | archive-date=2015-02-21 }}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last = Hartshorne|first = Robin|author-link = Robin Hartshorne|title = Geometry: Euclid and Beyond|year = 1997|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer-Verlag]]|section = Construction problems and field extensions: Cubic and quartic equations|isbn = 0-387-98650-2|zbl = 0954.51001}}</ref> (again, supposing that {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is a depressed quartic) is

:<math>R_3(y)=y^3+2a_2y^2+({a_2}^2-4a_0)y-{a_1}^2\text{.}</math>

The origin of this definition lies in another method of solving quartic equations, namely [[Quartic function#Descartes' solution|Descartes' method]]. If you try to find the roots of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} by expressing it as a product of two monic quadratic polynomials {{math|''x''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''αx''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''β''}} and {{math|''x''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;–&nbsp;''αx''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''γ''}}, then
:<math>P(x)=(x^2+\alpha x+\beta)(x^2-\alpha x+\gamma)\Longleftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}\beta+\gamma-\alpha^2=a_2\\ \alpha(-\beta+\gamma)=a_1\\ \beta\gamma=a_0.\end{array}\right.</math>

If there is a solution of this system with {{math|''α''&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0}} (note that if {{math|''a''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0}}, then this is automatically true for any solution), the previous system is equivalent to
:<math>\left\{\begin{array}{l}\beta+\gamma=a_2+\alpha^2\\-\beta+\gamma=\frac{a_1}{\alpha}\\ \beta\gamma=a_0.\end{array}\right.</math>

It is a consequence of the first two equations that then
:<math>\beta=\frac12\left(a_2+\alpha^2-\frac{a_1}{\alpha}\right)</math>
and
:<math>\gamma=\frac12\left(a_2+\alpha^2+\frac{a_1}{\alpha}\right).</math>
After replacing, in the third equation, {{math|''β''}} and {{math|''γ''}} by these values one gets that
:<math>\left(a_2+\alpha^2\right)^2-\frac{{a_1}^2}{\alpha^2}=4a_0\text{,}</math>
and this is equivalent to the assertion that {{math|''α''<sup>2</sup>}} is a root of {{math|''R''<sub>3</sub>(''y'')}}. So, again, knowing the roots of {{math|''R''<sub>3</sub>(''y'')}} helps to determine the roots of {{math|''P''(''x'')}}.

Note that
:<math>R_3(y)=R_1\left(\frac y2\right)\text{.}</math>

===Fourth definition===
Still another possible definition is<ref name="Kaplanski">{{Citation | last=Kaplansky | first=Irving | author-link=Irving Kaplansky | title = Fields and Rings | edition=2nd | zbl=1001.16500 | series=Chicago Lectures in Mathematics | publisher = [[University of Chicago Press]] | year = 1972 | isbn = 0-226-42451-0 | section = Fields: Cubic and quartic equations }}</ref>
:<math>R_4(y)=y^3-a_2y^2+(a_1a_3-4a_0)y+4a_0a_2-{a_1}^2-a_0{a_3}^2.</math>

In fact, if the roots of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} are {{math|''α''<sub>1</sub>, ''α''<sub>2</sub>, ''α''<sub>3</sub>}}, and {{math|''α''<sub>4</sub>}}, then

:<math>R_4(y)=\bigl(y-(\alpha_1\alpha_2+\alpha_3\alpha_4)\bigr)\bigl(y-(\alpha_1\alpha_3+\alpha_2\alpha_4)\bigr)\bigl(y-(\alpha_1\alpha_4+\alpha_2\alpha_3)\bigr)\text{,}</math>
a fact the follows from [[Vieta's formulas]]. In other words, ''R''<sub>4</sub>(''y'') is the monic polynomial whose roots are 
{{math|''α''<sub>1</sub>''α''<sub>2</sub> + ''α''<sub>3</sub>''α''<sub>4</sub>}}, 
{{math|''α''<sub>1</sub>''α''<sub>3</sub> + ''α''<sub>2</sub>''α''<sub>4</sub>}}, and 
{{math|''α''<sub>1</sub>''α''<sub>4</sub> + ''α''<sub>2</sub>''α''<sub>3</sub>}}.

It is easy to see that
:<math>\alpha_1\alpha_2+\alpha_3\alpha_4-(\alpha_1\alpha_3+\alpha_2\alpha_4)=(\alpha_1-\alpha_4)(\alpha_2-\alpha_3)\text{,}</math>
:<math>\alpha_1\alpha_3+\alpha_2\alpha_4-(\alpha_1\alpha_4+\alpha_2\alpha_3)=(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)(\alpha_3-\alpha_4)\text{,}</math>
:<math>\alpha_1\alpha_2+\alpha_3\alpha_4-(\alpha_1\alpha_4+\alpha_2\alpha_3)=(\alpha_1-\alpha_3)(\alpha_2-\alpha_4)\text{.}</math>
Therefore, {{math|''P''(''x'')}} has a [[Multiplicity (mathematics)#Multiplicity of a root of a polynomial|multiple root]] if and only if {{math|''R''<sub>4</sub>(''y'')}} has a multiple root. More precisely, {{math|''P''(''x'')}} and {{math|''R''<sub>4</sub>(''y'')}} have the same [[discriminant]].

If {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is a depressed polynomial, then

:<math>\begin{align}R_4(y)&=y^3-a_2y^2-4a_0y+4a_0a_2-{a_1}^2\\ &=R_2\left(\frac y2\right)\text{.}\end{align}</math>

===Fifth definition===
Yet another definition is<ref>{{Citation|last = Rotman|first=Joseph|title = Galois Theory|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer-Verlag]]|edition = 2nd|isbn = 0-387-98541-7|year = 1998|chapter = Galois groups of quadratics, cubics, and quartics|zbl = 0924.12001}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last = van der Waerden|first=Bartel Leendert|author-link = Bartel Leendert van der Waerden|title = [[Moderne Algebra|Algebra]]|volume = 1|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer-Verlag]]|edition = 7th|isbn = 0-387-97424-5|year = 1991|section = The Galois theory: Equations of the second, third, and fourth degrees|zbl = 0724.12001}}</ref>

:<math>R_5(y)=y^3-2a_2y^2+({a_2}^2+a_3a_1-4a_0)y+{a_1}^2-a_3a_2a_1+{a_3}^2a_0\text{.}</math>

If, as above, the roots of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} are {{math|''α''<sub>1</sub>, ''α''<sub>2</sub>, ''α''<sub>3</sub>}}, and {{math|''α''<sub>4</sub>}}, then

:<math>R_5(y)=\bigl(y-(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)(\alpha_3+\alpha_4)\bigr)\bigl(y-(\alpha_1+\alpha_3)(\alpha_2+\alpha_4)\bigr)\bigl(y-(\alpha_1+\alpha_4)(\alpha_2+\alpha_3)\bigr)\text{,}</math>
again as a consequence of [[Vieta's formulas]]. In other words, {{math|''R''<sub>5</sub>(''y'')}} is the monic polynomial whose roots are 
{{math|(''α''<sub>1</sub> + ''α''<sub>2</sub>)(''α''<sub>3</sub> + ''α''<sub>4</sub>)}},
{{math|(''α''<sub>1</sub> + ''α''<sub>3</sub>)(''α''<sub>2</sub> + ''α''<sub>4</sub>)}}, and 
{{math|(''α''<sub>1</sub> + ''α''<sub>4</sub>)(''α''<sub>2</sub> + ''α''<sub>3</sub>)}}.

It is easy to see that

:<math>(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)(\alpha_3+\alpha_4)-(\alpha_1+\alpha_3)(\alpha_2+\alpha_4)=-(\alpha_1-\alpha_4)(\alpha_2-\alpha_3)\text{,}</math>
:<math>(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)(\alpha_3+\alpha_4)-(\alpha_1+\alpha_4)(\alpha_2+\alpha_3)=-(\alpha_1-\alpha_3)(\alpha_2-\alpha_4)\text{,}</math>
:<math>(\alpha_1+\alpha_3)(\alpha_2+\alpha_4)-(\alpha_1+\alpha_4)(\alpha_2+\alpha_3)=-(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)(\alpha_3-\alpha_4)\text{.}</math>
Therefore, as it happens with {{math|''R''<sub>4</sub>(''y'')}}, {{math|''P''(''x'')}} has a multiple root if and only if {{math|''R''<sub>5</sub>(''y'')}} has a multiple root. More precisely, {{math|''P''(''x'')}} and {{math|''R''<sub>5</sub>(''y'')}} have the same discriminant. This is also a consequence of the fact that {{math|''R''<sub>5</sub>(''y''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''a''<sub>2</sub>)}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{math|-''R''<sub>4</sub>(-''y'')}}.

Note that if {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is a depressed polynomial, then

:<math>\begin{align}R_5(y)&=y^3-2a_2y^2+({a_2}^2-4a_0)y+{a_1}^2\\ &=-R_3(-y)\\ &=-R_1\left(-\frac y2\right)\text{.}\end{align}</math>

==Applications==
===Solving quartic equations===
It was explained above how {{math|[[Resolvent cubic#First definition|''R''<sub>1</sub>(''y'')]]}}, {{math|[[Resolvent cubic#Second definition|''R''<sub>2</sub>(''y'')]]}}, and {{math|[[Resolvent cubic#Third definition|''R''<sub>3</sub>(''y'')]]}} can be used to find the roots of {{math|''P''(''x'')}} if this polynomial is depressed. In the general case, one simply has to find the roots of the depressed polynomial {{math|''P''(''x''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>3</sub>/4)}}. For each root&nbsp;{{math|''x''<sub>0</sub>}} of this polynomial, {{math|''x''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>3</sub>/4}} is a root of&nbsp;{{math|''P''(''x'')}}.

===Factoring quartic polynomials===
If a quartic polynomial {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is [[Irreducible polynomial|reducible]] in {{math|''k''[''x'']}}, then it is the product of two quadratic polynomials or the product of a linear polynomial by a cubic polynomial. This second possibility occurs if and only if {{math|''P''(''x'')}} has a root in&nbsp;{{math|''k''}}. In order to determine whether or not {{math|''P''(''x'')}} can be expressed as the product of two quadratic polynomials, let us assume, for simplicity, that {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is a depressed polynomial. Then it was seen [[#Third definition|above]] that if the resolvent cubic {{math|''R''<sub>3</sub>(''y'')}} has a non-null root of the form {{math|''α''<sup>2</sup>}}, for some {{math|''α''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''k''}}, then such a decomposition exists.

This can be used to prove that, in {{math|'''R'''[''x'']}}, every quartic polynomial without real roots can be expressed as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Let {{math|''P''(''x'')}} be such a polynomial. We can assume [[without loss of generality]] that {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is monic. We can also assume without loss of generality that it is a reduced polynomial, because {{math|''P''(''x'')}} can be expressed as the product of two quadratic polynomials if and only if {{math|''P''(''x''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>3</sub>/4)}} can and this polynomial is a reduced one. Then {{math|''R''<sub>3</sub>(''y'')}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{math|''y''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;2''a''<sub>2</sub>''y''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;(''a''<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;4''a''<sub>0</sub>)''y''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>}}. There are two cases:
* If {{math|''a''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0}} then {{math|''R''<sub>3</sub>(0)}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{math|−''a''<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;<&nbsp;0}}. Since {{math|''R''<sub>3</sub>(''y'')&nbsp;>&nbsp;0}} if {{math|''y''}} is large enough, then, by the [[intermediate value theorem]], {{math|''R''<sub>3</sub>(''y'')}} has a root {{math|''y''<sub>0</sub>}} with {{math|''y''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;>&nbsp;0}}. So, we can take {{math|''α''}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{math|{{sqrt|''y''<sub>0</sub>}}}}.
* If {{math|''a''<sub>1</sub>}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{math|0}}, then {{math|''R''<sub>3</sub>(''y'')}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{math|''y''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;2''a''<sub>2</sub>''y''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;(''a''<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;4''a''<sub>0</sub>)''y''}}. The roots of this polynomial are&nbsp;{{math|0}} and the roots of the quadratic polynomial&nbsp;{{math|''y''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;2''a''<sub>2</sub>''y''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''a''<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;4''a''<sub>0</sub>}}. If {{math|''a''<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;4''a''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;<&nbsp;0}}, then the product of the two roots of this polynomial is smaller than&nbsp;{{math|0}} and therefore it has a root greater than&nbsp;{{math|0}} (which happens to be {{math|−''a''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;2{{sqrt|''a''<sub>0</sub>}}}}) and we can take {{math|''α''}} as the [[square root]] of that root. Otherwise, {{math|''a''<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;4''a''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0}} and then,
::<math>P(x)=\left(x^2+\frac{a_2+\sqrt{{a_2}^2-4a_0}}2\right)\left(x^2+\frac{a_2-\sqrt{{a_2}^2-4a_0}}2\right)\text{.}</math>

More generally, if {{math|''k''}} is a [[real closed field]], then every quartic polynomial without roots in {{math|''k''}} can be expressed as the product of two quadratic polynomials in {{math|''k''[''x'']}}. Indeed, this statement can be expressed in [[first-order logic]] and any such statement that holds for {{math|'''R'''}} also holds for any real closed field.

A similar approach can be used to get an algorithm<ref name="Brookfield"/> to determine whether or not a quartic polynomial {{math|''P''(''x'')&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''Q'''[''x'']}} is reducible and, if it is, how to express it as a product of polynomials of smaller degree. Again, we will suppose that&nbsp;{{math|''P''(''x'')}} is monic and depressed. Then&nbsp;{{math|''P''(''x'')}} is reducible if and only if at least one of the following conditions holds:
* The polynomial {{math|''P''(''x'')}} has a rational root (this can be determined using the [[rational root theorem]]).
* The resolvent cubic&nbsp;{{math|''R''<sub>3</sub>(''y'')}} has a root of the form {{math|''α''<sup>2</sup>}}, for some non-null rational number&nbsp;{{math|''α''}} (again, this can be determined using the [[rational root theorem]]).
* The number {{math|''a''<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;4''a''<sub>0</sub>}} is the square of a [[rational number]] and {{math|''a''<sub>1</sub>}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{math|0}}.
Indeed:
* If {{math|''P''(''x'')}} has a rational root {{math|''r''}}, then {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is the product of {{math|''x''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''r''}} by a cubic polynomial in {{math|'''Q'''[''x'']}}, which can be determined by [[polynomial long division]] or by [[Ruffini's rule]].
* If there is a rational number&nbsp;{{math|''α''&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0}} such that {{math|''α''<sup>2</sup>}} is a root of&nbsp;{{math|''R''<sub>3</sub>(''y'')}}, it was shown [[#Third definition|above]] how to express&nbsp;{{math|''P''(''x'')}} as the product of two quadratic polynomials in {{math|'''Q'''[''x'']}}.
* Finally, if the third condition holds and if {{math|''δ''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''Q'''}} is such that {{math|''δ''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;}}={{math|&nbsp;''a''<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;4''a''<sub>0</sub>}}, then {{math|''P''(''x'')}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{math|(''x''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;(''a''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''δ'')/2)(''x''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;(''a''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''δ'')/2)}}.

===Galois groups of irreducible quartic polynomials===
The resolvent cubic of an [[Irreducible polynomial|irreducible quartic polynomial]] {{math|''P''(''x'')}} can be used to determine its [[Galois group]] {{math|''G''}}; that is, the Galois group of the [[splitting field]] of {{math|''P''(''x'')}}. Let&nbsp;{{mvar|m}} be the [[Degree of a field extension|degree]] over {{mvar|k}} of the splitting field of the resolvent cubic (it can be either {{math|''R''<sub>4</sub>(''y'')}} or {{math|''R''<sub>5</sub>(''y'')}}; they have the same splitting field). Then the group&nbsp;{{mvar|G}} is a subgroup of the [[symmetric group]] {{math|''S''<sub>4</sub>}}. More precisely:<ref name="Kaplanski" />
* If {{math|''m'' {{=}} 1}} (that is, if the resolvent cubic factors into linear factors in&nbsp;{{mvar|k}}), then&nbsp;{{mvar|G}} is the group {{math|{''e'', (12)(34), (13)(24), (14)(23)}}}.
* If {{math|''m'' {{=}} 2}} (that is, if the resolvent cubic has one and, [[Multiplicity (mathematics)#Multiplicity of a root of a polynomial|up to multiplicity]], only one root in&nbsp;{{math|''k''}}), then, in order to determine&nbsp;{{mvar|G}}, one can determine whether or not {{math|''P''(''x'')}} is still irreducible after adjoining to the field {{mvar|k}} the roots of the resolvent cubic. If not, then {{mvar|G}} is a [[cyclic group]] of [[Order (group theory)|order]]&nbsp;4; more precisely, it is one of the three cyclic subgroups of&nbsp;{{math|''S''<sub>4</sub>}} generated by any of its six {{math|4}}-cycles. If it is still irreducible, then {{mvar|G}} is one of the three subgroups of&nbsp;{{math|''S''<sub>4</sub>}} of order&nbsp;{{math|8}}, each of which is isomorphic to the [[dihedral group]] of order&nbsp;{{math|8}}.
* If {{math|''m'' {{=}} 3}}, then {{mvar|G}} is the [[alternating group]] {{math|''A''<sub>4</sub>}}.
* If {{math|''m'' {{=}} 6}}, then {{mvar|G}} is the whole group {{math|''S''<sub>4</sub>}}.
